m102.text: Pip pushes his fridge door gently. It swings shut by itself, and stays closed. There is no lock and no catch. What keeps it closed?

m103.text: One, the cold air inside. Two, a strip of magnet. Three, sticky glue.

m201p.text: Today is our magnet hunt! Where are the magnets hiding in my home?

m204.text: A little honeybee is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

m205m.text: Bees love flowers. Check near the window!

m206.text: You against the Buddies! Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

h501.text: Are you ready? Three! Two! One! Go!

m401.text: Round one! What keeps Pip's fridge door closed? One, the cold air inside. Two, a strip of magnet. Three, sticky glue. Show me your fingers!

m403b.text: Three! The door is so hard to pull open. It must be glue!

m404p.text: Two. My steel spoon sticks to the door's soft edge.

m405m.text: Two. Glue would get messy, and cold air cannot hold a door.

m501.text: Be the magnetic strip! Shrink down. Quietly.

m502.text: You are a long, thin magnet, hidden inside the soft edge of the fridge door. You go all the way round the door.

m503.text: The door swings. The fridge's steel body comes closer. You pull towards it, and the edge presses on it, snug.

m504.text: The door stays closed. The cold air stays in.

m601.text: The answer is two: a strip of magnet! Did you show two fingers? Put one finger up!

m602p.text: A magnetic strip is a long, thin magnet, such as the strip hidden inside our fridge door's soft edge!

m701b.text: But where is the magnet? I can't see it!

m702.text: Look closer. Inside the door's soft edge is a long magnetic strip. It goes all the way round the door.

m703.text: The fridge's body is made of steel. The strip is attracted to the steel, so the door stays closed, and the cold air stays in.

m705.text: Strips of magnets can be found inside the doors of a refrigerator. These help to keep the door closed.

m801b.text: Magnets stick to anything shiny! So my magnet will stick to this shiny window frame!

m802.text: Something is not right. If you can spot it, cross your arms. Hold on!

m804m.text: The window frame is made of aluminium. Aluminium is not a magnetic material, so the magnet is not attracted to it.

m805.text: Shiny is not the clue. Only magnetic materials, like iron and steel, are attracted.

m901b.text: A whiteboard looks like plastic. So why does my magnet stick to it?

m902.text: Look closer. Under the white writing surface is a thin sheet of steel. The magnet is attracted to the steel sheet.

m903s.text: Some whiteboards have steel sheets under the writing surfaces. These allow magnets to be attracted to the whiteboards.

m904m.text: A magnetic whiteboard is a whiteboard with a steel sheet under its writing surface, such as the little board on Pip's kitchen wall!

m905.text: And look at Pip's bedroom door. A gust of wind blows in, but the door does not slam. The magnet on the doorstop holds the door's steel plate.

m906b.text: A magnetic doorstop is a doorstop with a magnet that holds the door open, such as the one by Pip's bedroom door!

m908.text: The magnet on a doorstop helps to hold the door in place and prevents it from closing suddenly.

m1001.text: Show me your score hand! Two fingers? You beat the Buddies. High five!

m1002.text: Did you spot the honeybee? It was on the edge of the curtain!

m1003m.text: Here is a fun fact! Scientists think honeybees can feel the Earth's magnetism, a little like a compass inside them!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?

m1101p.text: Look at this train! It floats above its track, with no wheels touching!

m1102.text: How can a train float? Find out in Part Two!
